intro: Serenbe is a community of farm, woods and creeks in Chattahoochee Hills, in the hills south-west of Atlanta, Georgia. A reader who knows its woods sent us two trees from it: a loblolly pine with a candelabra crown that stands out among ranks of straight, thin pines, and a pale beech leaning over a small waterfall on a granite slab. We know neither tree's age yet, and we would like to.

trees.story:
"Grandfather Pine," the reader called it when they sent us this tree from Serenbe, in the hills south-west of Atlanta, with a GPS fix taken at its foot.

The photograph shows why. It is a loblolly pine, the common timber pine of the Southeast, and most of them in this wood stand tall and straight in ranks, each a single thin column. This one broke the pattern. Its trunk is short and thick, armoured in big plates of red-brown bark, and a few metres up it divides into a crowd of heavy limbs that twist and fork and lift away from each other like the arms of a candelabra, some of them snapped and healed. A pine grows like that when it has had room and light for a long time, and the crowd of straight young pines around it shows how much room it had.

We have no age or girth for it. If you know how old it is, or have measured it, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Stand well back from the foot of it and look up to see how all the limbs leave the trunk.

trees.story:
A reader who knows the woods at Serenbe, in the hills south-west of Atlanta, sent us this beech as "Grandmother Beech", with a GPS fix taken where they stood.

It stands where a creek slides over a broad slab of granite and drops in a thin waterfall, and the tree has taken the view for itself. The trunk is smooth and pale grey, the way beech bark always is, and it leans out over the water before dividing into a wide, open crown, with one long limb stretching almost level across the rock. In the reader's winter photograph the crown is bare, but a scatter of copper leaves is still hanging on, as beech leaves famously do until spring pushes them off.

We do not know how old it is or how thick the trunk measures. The reader gave us the name and the place, and we would be glad of anything else you know about it.

Come in winter or early spring, when the bare crown shows its full spread against the sky.

question_meta: Two trees at Serenbe, Georgia: where the candelabra pine and the waterfall beech stand, and what we still want to know.
question_answer: The two trees we know at Serenbe, Georgia, are Grandfather Pine and Grandmother Beech, both in the woods of Chattahoochee Hills, south-west of Atlanta. Check which paths are open before you go.
question_context: A reader sent us photographs of two trees from the woods at Serenbe, a community in Chattahoochee Hills south-west of Atlanta, each with a GPS fix taken where they stood. Grandfather Pine is a loblolly pine whose short thick trunk splits into a spray of crooked limbs while the pines around it stand tall and straight. Grandmother Beech is a smooth grey American beech leaning over a creek where a small waterfall slides across a granite slab, with copper leaves still on its bare winter branches. The two stand about a mile and a half apart. We have no measured girth or age for either, and no register entry within a hundred metres of them. Serenbe keeps its trails for residents and guests of the Inn at Serenbe, and opens them to the public twice a year for the Serenbe Trail Race. Readers who know the trees can add what they know on each tree's page, and anyone who visits can send a photograph taken at the foot of either one so that we can check the pin.
